topics.title: Clauses and complex sentences
topics.intro: A main clause makes sense on its own. A subordinate clause (because the storm rose, although Theo was tired) depends on it. Controlling clauses lets you build sentences that carry real thought.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between a compound and a complex sentence, with an example of each.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to turn two short sentences about a myth into one complex sentence.
topics.hook: A main clause can stand alone; a subordinate clause leans on it and cannot.

visual.caption: Simple: one main clause. Compound: two main clauses joined by a FANBOYS word. Complex: a main clause plus a subordinate clause that cannot stand alone.

topics.title: Relative clauses and parenthesis
topics.intro: Relative clauses (who, which, that, whose, where) add detail to a noun. Parenthesis adds an extra idea with commas, brackets or dashes, and each choice changes the tone.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between a defining and a non-defining relative clause.
topics.talk: Find a sentence with brackets in a newspaper and ask {him} why the writer used brackets rather than commas.
topics.hook: Brackets whisper, commas talk, dashes shout: choose the volume of your extra detail.

parts: who was born from Zeus’s head
who was born from Zeus’s head,

visual.caption: A defining clause tells you which one. A non-defining clause adds extra information and could be lifted out.

topics.title: Verbs: passive, modal and subjunctive
topics.intro: The passive voice puts the receiver of the action first (the Minotaur was slain). Modal verbs show certainty or possibility. The subjunctive (if I were, I insist that she be) marks formal or hypothetical writing.
topics.teach: Explain when a writer might choose the passive voice on purpose.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to rewrite “Theseus killed the Minotaur” in the passive, then explain what changes.
topics.hook: In the passive, the doer can vanish: “Mistakes were made.” By whom?

visual.caption: Active to passive: the receiver moves to the front, the verb becomes “was” + past participle, and the doer becomes the agent after “by”.

topics.title: Semicolons, colons, dashes and hyphens
topics.intro: Semicolons join closely related main clauses; colons introduce what follows; dashes interrupt; hyphens join words. Accurate punctuation is what separates good writing from excellent writing.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between a semicolon and a colon, with an example of each.
topics.talk: Write a sentence with a deliberate punctuation mistake and let {him} find and fix it.
topics.hook: A semicolon is a soft full stop; a colon is a drum roll before the reveal.

visual.caption: A semicolon balances two main clauses; a colon needs a main clause before it; a dash interrupts; a hyphen joins.

topics.title: Speech, reported speech and register
topics.intro: Direct speech quotes the words; reported speech retells them and usually shifts the tense back. Standard English and the right register (formal or informal) matter in every exam answer.
topics.teach: Explain how “I am leaving tomorrow,” said Kit changes in reported speech.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to say the same request formally and informally.
topics.hook: Reported speech steps back in time: “I am tired” becomes “he said he was tired”.

head: Direct speech
Reported speech
rows: The captain said that they **would** sail the next day.
visual.caption: No speech marks; the tense shifts back, and pronouns and time words change (we → they, tomorrow → the next day).

topics.title: Greek roots
topics.intro: Thousands of English words are built from Ancient Greek: tele (far) + phone (sound), demos (people) + kratos (power). Knowing the roots means you can decode words you have never seen.
topics.teach: Work out the meaning of “chronophobia” from its roots.
topics.talk: Pick a long word on a cereal box or in the news and decode its Greek roots together.
topics.hook: Learn one root, unlock a dozen words: tele (far) gives telephone, telescope and television.

visual.caption: Greek building blocks: learn the parts and you can decode words you have never seen.

topics.title: Latin roots and etymology
topics.intro: English also borrowed thousands of Latin roots: port (carry), spect (look), scrib (write). Some words even mix Greek and Latin.
topics.teach: Explain why “television” is called a hybrid word.
topics.talk: Ask {him} for three words containing “port” and what each one has to do with carrying.
topics.hook: Port means carry: a porter carries your bags, and portable things can be carried.

visual.caption: Latin roots with prefixes snapped on the front.

topics.title: Words from Greek myth
topics.intro: Echo, panic, nemesis, tantalise, odyssey: the myths live on inside everyday English. Each word carries its story with it.
topics.teach: Explain where the word “tantalise” comes from and why it fits.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to tell you the myth behind “narcissist” or “Achilles heel”.
topics.hook: Every myth word hides a story: panic, echo, tantalise, odyssey.

topics.title: Academic vocabulary
topics.intro: Precise, sophisticated words make an argument sharper: hubris, laconic, ominous, poignant. Many come from Greek, so you can link them to your Greek lessons.
topics.teach: Use three of today’s words correctly in one paragraph about a myth.
topics.talk: Challenge each other to use one new word naturally at dinner.
topics.hook: Precise words save sentences: “laconic” says “using very few words” in one go.

topics.title: Rhetoric and persuasion
topics.intro: Aristotle named the three appeals: ethos (trust), pathos (emotion) and logos (logic). Great speakers combine them with devices such as anaphora, antithesis and the rule of three.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between ethos, pathos and logos, with an example of each.
topics.talk: Watch a short political speech or advert together and ask {him} which appeal it relies on most.
topics.hook: Ethos, pathos, logos: trust me, feel this, think about it.

head: Appeal
Persuades through
Example
rows: “As a doctor for twenty years, I have seen…”
“Three in five rivers fail safety tests…”
visual.caption: Aristotle’s three appeals. The best speakers combine all three.

topics.title: Writing craft
topics.intro: Strong narrative writing is designed: an opening that hooks, sentences that vary for effect, tension that builds, and details that show rather than tell.
topics.teach: Explain how a writer can build tension using sentence length.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to describe the room using only details, without naming a single emotion.
topics.hook: Show, don’t tell: trembling hands beat “she was scared”.

visual.caption: Freytag’s pyramid: tension rises to the climax, then falls away.

topics.title: Tricky spellings
topics.intro: Some words catch out even confident writers: necessary, separate, embarrass, rhythm. Learn the trick for each one.
topics.teach: Explain a trick for remembering how to spell “necessary”.
topics.talk: Test {him} on three of today’s words in the car.
topics.hook: Every tricky word has a trick: find it, say it, remember it.

topics.title: GCSE language analysis
topics.intro: GCSE English Language rewards precise terminology: semantic field, connotation, juxtaposition, sibilance, asyndetic lists. The skill is linking each method to its effect on the reader.
topics.teach: Explain what a semantic field is and how it creates an effect.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to find a semantic field in a song lyric or advert.
topics.hook: Method + evidence + effect: name it, quote it, explain what it does to the reader.

topics.title: Comparing non-fiction texts
topics.intro: GCSE questions ask you to compare writers’ viewpoints and methods across two texts, often from different centuries. You need comparative connectives and a sense of each writer’s purpose and audience.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between summarising two texts and comparing them.
topics.talk: Read two reviews of the same film and ask {him} how their viewpoints differ.
topics.hook: Compare means linking: find the similarity, then explore the difference.

topics.title: Punctuation for effect
topics.intro: At the top level, punctuation is a tool for meaning and rhythm: an ellipsis that trails off, a colon that delivers a reveal, a single-word sentence that lands like a blow.
topics.teach: Explain how a writer might use a colon to create a dramatic reveal.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to rewrite a dull sentence about a monster using one punctuation mark for effect.
topics.hook: Punctuation is a conductor’s baton: it controls the rhythm, the pauses and the punch.

items.prompt: Which of these is a main clause (it makes sense on its own)?

options.text: the Cyclops slept
because the Cyclops slept
options.feedback: “because” makes it depend on another clause.

options.text: while the Cyclops slept
options.feedback: “while” turns it into a subordinate clause.

items.explain: A main clause has a subject and a verb and makes sense alone.
items.hook: Test it: could it be a sentence on its own, with a full stop? Then it is a main clause.

items.prompt: In “Although the sea was wild, Odysseus kept sailing”, which part is the subordinate clause?

options.text: Although the sea was wild
Odysseus kept sailing
options.feedback: That is the main clause: it makes sense on its own.

options.text: the sea
options.feedback: That is a noun phrase, not a clause: it has no verb.

items.explain: The subordinating conjunction “although” makes the first clause depend on the main clause.
items.hook: A subordinating conjunction (although, because, when) makes a clause lean on another.

visual.caption: The subordinate clause depends on the main clause: on its own it is not a sentence.

items.prompt: Which is a compound sentence?

options.text: Theo opened the door, but the room was empty.
When Theo opened the door, the room was empty.
options.feedback: That is complex: “When…” is subordinate.

options.text: Theo opened the door.
options.feedback: That is simple: one main clause.

items.explain: A compound sentence joins two main clauses with a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so).
items.hook: FANBOYS join two equals: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.

visual.caption: Two main clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction.

items.prompt: Which is a complex sentence?

options.text: Because the oracle had spoken, the king was afraid.
The oracle spoke and the king was afraid of the prophecy.
options.feedback: Two main clauses joined by “and”: that is compound.

options.text: The oracle spoke. The king was afraid.
options.feedback: Two simple sentences.

items.explain: A complex sentence contains a main clause and at least one subordinate clause.
items.hook: Complex = main clause + subordinate clause. Compound = two main clauses.

visual.caption: Simple: one main clause. Compound: two main clauses joined by a FANBOYS word. Complex: a main clause plus a subordinate clause that cannot stand alone.

items.prompt: The coordinating conjunctions are remembered as FANBOYS. What does the Y stand for?
items.explain: For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So.
items.hook: FANBOYS: For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So.

items.prompt: Which word is a subordinating conjunction?

options.text: unless
but
options.feedback: “but” is coordinating (FANBOYS).

options.text: however
options.feedback: “however” is an adverb; it cannot join clauses on its own without a semicolon.

items.explain: Subordinating conjunctions include because, although, unless, while, since, if, when, until.
items.hook: A subordinating conjunction starts a clause that cannot stand alone: “unless you hurry…”

items.prompt: Which sentence contains a comma splice (an error)?

options.text: The gods were angry, they sent a storm.
The gods were angry, so they sent a storm.
options.feedback: A comma plus a coordinating conjunction is correct.

options.text: The gods were angry; they sent a storm.
options.feedback: A semicolon can join two main clauses.

items.explain: A comma alone cannot join two main clauses. Use a full stop, a semicolon, or a comma with a conjunction.
items.hook: A comma is too weak to hold two sentences together: use a full stop, a semicolon or a FANBOYS word.

items.prompt: Moving the subordinate clause to the front (“Although she was terrified, Mira stepped forward”) does what?

options.text: Delays the main action, building suspense
Makes the sentence a grammatical error
options.feedback: It is correct, with a comma after the subordinate clause.

options.text: Changes the sentence into a question
options.feedback: It is still a statement.

items.explain: Starting with the subordinate clause makes the reader wait for the main action.
items.example: “Although they were two goals down, the team fought back”: sports reports love this delay.

items.prompt: A group of words without a verb, such as “under the ancient olive tree”, is called a…
items.explain: A clause has a verb; a phrase does not. This one is a prepositional phrase.
items.hook: Clause = has a verb; phrase = no verb. No verb, no clause.

items.prompt: “Silence. Then a roar.” These are minor sentences. What makes them minor?

options.text: They have no main verb
They are missing a full stop
options.feedback: They do end with full stops; what they lack is a main verb.

options.text: They are used only in speech
options.feedback: Minor sentences appear in all kinds of writing, not just speech.

items.explain: Minor sentences lack a main verb. Used deliberately, they create pace and drama.
items.example: Adverts and film posters love minor sentences: “Coming soon.” “Ready when you are.”

items.prompt: In “What the Sphinx asked baffled every traveller”, what job does “What the Sphinx asked” do?

options.text: A noun clause acting as the subject
A relative clause describing the Sphinx
options.feedback: It does not describe a noun; it IS the subject.

options.text: An adverbial clause of time
options.feedback: It does not tell us when something happened; it names what was asked and acts as the subject.

items.explain: A noun clause can do the job of a noun: here, the subject of “baffled”.

items.prompt: Which sentence is an imperative?

options.text: Never look back at the underworld.
Orpheus never looked back again.
options.feedback: That is declarative: a statement.

options.text: Why did Orpheus look back?
options.feedback: That is interrogative: a question.

items.explain: Imperatives give commands and usually start with a verb.
items.hook: Four sentence types: statement, question, command, exclamation.
items.example: Road signs are imperatives: “Stop.” “Give way.” “Keep left.”

items.prompt: Complete: “Medusa, ___ gaze turned people to stone, lived on a distant island.”
items.explain: “whose” shows possession: her gaze. “who’s” means “who is”.
items.hook: Who’s = who is. If “who is” does not fit, write whose.

items.prompt: Complete formally: “The hero ___ the gods favoured was Perseus.”
items.explain: Use “whom” when the person is the object of the verb: the gods favoured him → whom.
items.hook: He → who, him → whom: both him and whom end in m.

items.prompt: Which sentence has a NON-defining relative clause?

options.text: Athena, who was born from Zeus’s head, was goddess of wisdom.
The goddess who was born from Zeus’s head was Athena.
options.feedback: This clause identifies which goddess: it is defining, so no commas.

options.text: The goddess that sprang from Zeus was Athena.
options.feedback: Defining again: it picks her out.

items.explain: A non-defining clause adds extra information and sits inside commas; you could remove it and still know who is meant.
items.hook: Non-defining = extra information in commas: lift it out and the sentence still works.

parts: who was born from Zeus’s head
who was born from Zeus’s head,

visual.caption: A defining clause tells you which one. A non-defining clause adds extra information and could be lifted out.

items.prompt: Which is correct?

options.text: The sword, which was bronze, shone.
The sword, that was bronze, shone.
options.feedback: “that” is not used in non-defining clauses (the ones inside commas).

options.text: The sword which, was bronze shone.
options.feedback: The commas must go around the whole clause.

items.explain: In non-defining clauses, use “which” (for things) or “who” (for people), never “that”.
items.hook: Commas round the clause? Then use which or who, never that.

items.prompt: “The soldiers who were exhausted surrendered.” vs “The soldiers, who were exhausted, surrendered.” What is the difference?

options.text: First: only the exhausted ones surrendered. Second: all did, and all were exhausted.
First: all surrendered. Second: only the exhausted ones surrendered.
options.feedback: The commas change the meaning completely.

options.text: No difference: the commas only show where to pause for breath.
options.feedback: Both are correct, but mean different things.

items.explain: Commas turn a defining clause (which soldiers?) into extra information about all of them.
items.hook: No commas = only some of them; commas = all of them.

items.prompt: Complete: “Delphi, ___ the oracle spoke, was the centre of the Greek world.”
items.explain: “where” introduces a relative clause about a place.

items.prompt: Which punctuation for parenthesis makes the extra information feel the MOST like a quiet aside?

options.text: brackets
dashes
options.feedback: Dashes tend to make the extra information more dramatic or emphatic.

options.text: commas
options.feedback: Commas are the most neutral; brackets feel more like a whisper.

items.explain: Brackets: aside. Commas: neutral. Dashes: emphatic.
items.hook: Brackets whisper, commas talk, dashes shout.

items.prompt: Why might a writer choose dashes here: “The Minotaur – half man, half bull – waited in the dark”?

options.text: To make the description more dramatic
Because commas would be a grammatical error
options.feedback: Commas would be correct too; dashes are a stylistic choice.

options.text: To show that letters have been left out
options.feedback: That is the job of an apostrophe.

items.explain: A pair of dashes makes the parenthesis stand out.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

options.text: Kit, who hated heights, climbed Mount Olympus.
Kit, who hated heights climbed Mount Olympus.
options.feedback: Parenthetical commas come in pairs: you need one after “heights”.

options.text: Kit who hated heights, climbed up Mount Olympus.
options.feedback: You need a comma before “who” as well.

items.explain: Parenthesis needs punctuation at both ends.
items.hook: Parenthesis is a sandwich: punctuation on both sides of the filling.

items.prompt: In “Hermes, the messenger of the gods, wore winged sandals”, what is “the messenger of the gods”?

options.text: A noun phrase in apposition
A relative clause about Hermes
options.feedback: There is no relative pronoun or verb: it is a noun phrase.

options.text: The subject of the sentence
options.feedback: The main clause is “Hermes wore winged sandals”.

items.explain: An appositive renames the noun next to it; it sits in commas like parenthesis.
items.hook: Apposition comes from Latin for “placing beside”: a second name parked next to the first.

items.prompt: Which sentence is in the passive voice?

options.text: The ship was wrecked by the storm.
The storm wrecked the ship.
options.feedback: That is active: the storm (the doer) is the subject.

options.text: The ship sailed straight into the storm.
options.feedback: That is active.

items.explain: In the passive, the thing affected becomes the subject, often with “was/were … by”.
items.hook: The zombie test: if you can add “by zombies” after the verb, it is passive. “The ship was wrecked by zombies.”

visual.caption: Active to passive: the receiver moves to the front, the verb becomes “was” + past participle, and the doer becomes the agent after “by”.

items.prompt: Why might a newspaper write “Mistakes were made” instead of “The minister made mistakes”?

options.text: The passive hides who was responsible
The passive is always more polite
options.feedback: It is not always polite; here it avoids blame.

options.text: The active voice is wrong
options.feedback: Both are grammatical.

items.explain: The passive can leave out the agent entirely, which can dodge responsibility.
items.example: “Mistakes were made” has been used by so many politicians that it has become a famous dodge.

visual.caption: In the passive the agent can simply disappear: nobody is named.

items.prompt: In “Troy was captured by the Greeks”, the Greeks are called the…
items.explain: The agent is the doer of the action in a passive sentence, introduced by “by”.
items.hook: The agent is the doer, like an agent who does the job. In the passive, it comes after “by”.

visual.caption: Active to passive: the receiver moves to the front, the verb becomes “was” + past participle, and the doer becomes the agent after “by”.

items.prompt: Which modal verb shows the STRONGEST certainty?

options.text: must
might
options.feedback: “might” shows possibility, not certainty.

options.text: could
options.feedback: “could” shows possibility.

items.explain: Modal verbs on a scale: might, may, could (possible) → should (likely) → will, must (certain).
items.hook: The certainty scale: might → may → could → should → will → must.

items.prompt: Find the modal verb: “You should never trust a gift from the Greeks.”

options.text: should
trust
options.feedback: “trust” is the main verb.

options.text: never
options.feedback: “never” is an adverb.

items.explain: Modal verbs (can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would) sit before a main verb.
items.hook: The nine modals: can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses the subjunctive correctly?

options.text: If I were a god, I would calm the sea.
If I was a god, I would calm the sea.
options.feedback: “was” is common in speech, but the formal subjunctive is “were”.

options.text: If I am a god, I would calm the stormy sea.
options.feedback: The tenses do not match.

items.explain: Hypothetical “if” clauses use the subjunctive “were” in formal writing.
items.example: “If I were you…” is the subjunctive we all use when giving advice.

items.prompt: Which is the formal subjunctive?

options.text: The oracle demanded that the king leave the city.
The oracle demanded that the king leaves the city.
options.feedback: After “demand that”, the subjunctive uses the bare verb: leave.

options.text: The oracle demanded that the king left the city.
options.feedback: Not the subjunctive.

items.explain: After verbs like demand, insist, recommend + that, the subjunctive uses the base form: that he leave, that she be.
items.hook: After demand, insist or recommend that, use the bare verb: “that he leave”, “that she be”.

items.prompt: Which sentence keeps the tense consistent?

options.text: Theo ran to the temple and knocked on the door.
Theo ran to the temple and knocks on the door.
options.feedback: “knocks” jumps into the present.

options.text: Theo runs to the temple and knocked on the door.
options.feedback: “runs” is present but “knocked” is past.

items.explain: Keep the same tense unless the time really changes.
items.hook: Pick a tense and stay in its lane.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses the past perfect (an action before another past action)?

options.text: By the time Kit arrived, the ship had sailed.
When Kit arrived, the ship was sailing away.
options.feedback: That is the past progressive (was sailing): the two events overlap rather than one coming first.

options.text: By tomorrow, Kit will have reached the ship.
options.feedback: That is the future perfect (will have reached).

items.explain: The past perfect (had + past participle) shows which past event came first.
items.hook: Past perfect = the past of the past: “had sailed” happened first.

items.prompt: “The Sirens were singing as the ship approached.” What does the progressive form suggest?

options.text: The singing was ongoing as the ship approached
The singing had finished before the ship arrived
options.feedback: That would be “had sung”.

options.text: The singing began only once the ship arrived
options.feedback: The progressive shows the singing was already going on before the ship got there.

items.explain: Progressive forms (was/were + -ing) show an action in progress.
items.hook: -ing for ongoing: “were singing” means still in progress.

items.prompt: Where is the semicolon used correctly?

options.text: Athena was wise; Ares was reckless.
Athena was wise; and Ares was reckless.
options.feedback: Do not use a conjunction after a semicolon joining two clauses.

options.text: Athena; was wise and Ares was reckless.
options.feedback: A semicolon must join two complete clauses.

items.explain: A semicolon joins two closely related main clauses without a conjunction.
items.hook: A semicolon is a soft full stop: both halves must be full sentences.

items.prompt: Why are semicolons used in this list? “The guests were Zeus, king of the gods; Poseidon, god of the sea; and Hades, lord of the underworld.”

options.text: The items already contain commas
Semicolons are always used in lists
options.feedback: Only when items contain commas.

options.text: To show each god is less important
options.feedback: Punctuation does not rank the items; the semicolons separate items that already contain commas.

items.explain: In a complex list, semicolons stop the commas getting confused.
items.hook: In a list whose items already contain commas, semicolons act as super-commas.

items.prompt: Which colon is used correctly?

options.text: The hero had one weakness: his heel.
The hero had: one weakness, his heel.
options.feedback: A colon must follow a complete clause, not split a verb from its object.

options.text: The: hero had one weakness.
options.feedback: That splits the sentence randomly.

items.explain: A colon comes after a complete clause and introduces an explanation, list, example or reveal.
items.hook: A colon is a drum roll: a complete sentence first, then the reveal.

items.prompt: What must come BEFORE a colon?
items.explain: If the words before the colon could not stand alone as a sentence, the colon is wrong.
items.hook: Cover everything after the colon: what is left must stand as a sentence.

visual.caption: Before a colon: a complete main clause.

items.prompt: What is a single dash doing here? “He opened the box – and instantly regretted it.”

options.text: Creating a dramatic pause before a twist
Joining two words into a compound
options.feedback: That is a hyphen’s job.

options.text: Introducing a list of what was in the box
options.feedback: Lists are introduced by colons.

items.explain: A single dash adds an afterthought, an interruption or a dramatic turn.

items.prompt: “A man eating shark” and “a man-eating shark”. Why does the hyphen matter?

options.text: Without it, the man is the one eating the shark
It doesn’t: both mean a shark that eats men
options.feedback: It changes who is eating whom!

options.text: The hyphen just makes the phrase look formal
options.feedback: Hyphens join words into a single description.

items.explain: Hyphens join compound adjectives before a noun: a well-known myth, a six-headed monster.
items.example: A man-eating shark is dangerous; a man eating shark is just having lunch.

visual.caption: With the hyphen, the shark eats men.

items.prompt: Which needs a hyphen?

options.text: a twelve-year-old girl
the girl is twelve years old
options.feedback: After the noun, no hyphens are needed.

options.text: twelve old years
options.feedback: This is not a compound adjective.

items.explain: Hyphenate a compound adjective before the noun (a twelve-year-old girl), not after it.
items.hook: Before the noun, hyphens join: a twelve-year-old girl. After it, they vanish: she is twelve years old.

items.prompt: Why does “re-cover the sofa” have a hyphen?

options.text: So it is not read as “recover” (get better)
Every word beginning with re- needs a hyphen
options.feedback: Most do not: rebuild, rewrite.

options.text: It is a mistake: it should be one word
options.feedback: It is correct and useful here.

items.explain: Some prefixes take a hyphen to avoid ambiguity: re-cover, re-sign (sign again) vs resign.
items.hook: re-cover (cover again) or recover (get better); re-sign (sign again) or resign (quit).

items.prompt: Which is correct?

options.text: The Hydra grew back its heads.
The Hydra grew back it’s heads.
options.feedback: “it’s” means “it is” or “it has”.

options.text: The Hydra grew back its’ heads.
options.feedback: “its’” is never correct.

items.explain: Possessive “its” has no apostrophe, like his and hers.
items.hook: It’s = it is or it has. Its = belonging to it, like his and hers: no apostrophe.

items.prompt: Which correctly shows the shields belonging to many warriors?

options.text: the warriors’ shields
the warrior’s shields
options.feedback: That means one warrior’s shields.

options.text: the warriors shield’s
options.feedback: The apostrophe belongs to the owners, not the thing owned.

items.explain: Plural ending in s: put the apostrophe after the s.
items.hook: Write the owners first, then add the apostrophe: warriors + ’ = warriors’.

items.prompt: Which is correct?

options.text: the children’s myths
the childrens’ myths
options.feedback: “children” is already plural without an s, so add ’s.

options.text: the childrens myths
options.feedback: You need an apostrophe for possession.

items.explain: Irregular plurals that do not end in s take ’s: children’s, women’s, people’s.
items.hook: Write the owner word, then add ’s: children + ’s = children’s.

items.prompt: Which of these is acceptable for something belonging to Achilles?

options.text: Achilles’ armour
Achille’s armour
options.feedback: The apostrophe must come after the full name.

items.hook: Poignant comes from an old French word for “pricking”: a sadness that stings.

items.prompt: What does “juxtaposition” mean?
items.answer: placing two contrasting things side by side
distractors: repeating a sound at the start of words
a long speech given by one character
items.explain: juxtaposition: placing two contrasting things side by side. The juxtaposition of the feast and the beggar made the hall feel cruel.
items.learn:
**juxtaposition**: placing two contrasting things side by side.
_The juxtaposition of the feast and the beggar made the hall feel cruel._
items.hook: Latin juxta = next to: two contrasting things placed side by side.

items.prompt: What does “ambiguous” mean?
items.answer: open to more than one interpretation
distractors: perfectly clear with only one meaning
very loud and hard to ignore
untrue or made up on purpose
items.explain: ambiguous: open to more than one interpretation. The oracle’s answers were always ambiguous.
items.learn:
**ambiguous**: open to more than one interpretation.
_The oracle’s answers were always ambiguous._
items.hook: Ambi = both: an ambiguous answer faces both ways.
items.example: Headlines can be ambiguous by accident: “Police help dog bite victim.”

items.prompt: What does “vindicate” mean?
items.answer: to prove someone right or innocent
distractors: to blame someone for a crime
to forget an insult or wrong
items.explain: vindicate: to prove someone right or innocent. The new evidence vindicated Theo.
items.learn:
**vindicate**: to prove someone right or innocent.
_The new evidence vindicated Theo._

items.prompt: What does “paradox” mean?
items.answer: a statement that seems to contradict itself
distractors: a simple fact that everyone accepts
a pair of lines that rhyme
a lie told to win an argument
items.explain: paradox: a statement that seems to contradict itself. “I know that I know nothing” is a famous paradox attributed to Socrates.
items.learn:
**paradox**: a statement that seems to contradict itself.
_“I know that I know nothing” is a famous paradox attributed to Socrates._
items.example: “Less is more” is an everyday paradox.

items.prompt: Which appeal is ETHOS?

options.text: Persuading through the speaker’s credibility
Persuading through the audience’s emotions
options.feedback: That is pathos.

options.text: Persuading through logic and evidence
options.feedback: That is logos.

items.explain: Aristotle’s three appeals: ethos (trust), pathos (emotion), logos (logic).
items.hook: Ethos, pathos, logos: trust in the speaker, feelings, and logic.
items.example: Adverts that feature a famous athlete or a doctor in a white coat are relying on ethos.

Persuades through
Example

items.prompt: “Imagine a child, cold and alone, waiting for help that never comes.” Which appeal is this?

options.text: pathos
logos
options.feedback: There is no evidence or reasoning: it targets feelings.

options.text: ethos
options.feedback: It does not rely on the speaker’s authority.

items.explain: Pathos stirs the audience’s emotions.
items.hook: Pathos = feeling, as in sympathy: it tugs at the heart.
items.example: Charity adverts that show one cold, lonely animal are using pathos.

items.prompt: “Three in five rivers fail safety tests; cleaning them would cost less than treating the illnesses they cause.” Which appeal?

options.text: logos
pathos
options.feedback: It relies on data and reasoning.

options.text: ethos
options.feedback: It does not mention the speaker’s credentials.

items.explain: Logos uses facts, statistics and logical argument.
items.hook: Logos = logic: facts, figures and reasons.

items.prompt: “We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields…” What device is Churchill using?

options.text: anaphora
onomatopoeia
options.feedback: There are no sound words.

options.text: oxymoron
options.feedback: No contradictory pairing.

items.explain: Anaphora (repeating words at the start of clauses) builds rhythm and determination. Churchill, June 1940.
items.hook: Anaphora: the same words at the start of each clause, like a drumbeat.
items.example: Churchill gave this speech in the House of Commons on 4 June 1940, just after the Dunkirk evacuation.

items.prompt: “That’s one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.” What device?

options.text: antithesis
alliteration
options.feedback: The power comes from the contrast of small/giant, man/mankind.

options.text: rhetorical question
options.feedback: It is a statement.

items.explain: Antithesis sets opposites side by side in parallel phrases.
items.example: Neil Armstrong said this as he became the first person to step onto the Moon, in July 1969.

items.prompt: “Ask not what your country can do for you – ask what you can do for your country.” This reversed structure is called…

options.text: chiasmus
anaphora
options.feedback: Anaphora repeats openings; this reverses the order.

options.text: hyperbole
options.feedback: Nothing is exaggerated.

items.explain: Chiasmus (from the Greek letter chi, X) reverses the order of words in the second half. John F. Kennedy, 1961.
items.hook: Chiasmus is named after the Greek letter chi (X): the words cross over, A B, B A.

items.prompt: “Veni, vidi, vici” (I came, I saw, I conquered) is a famous example of…

options.text: the rule of three (tricolon)
a rhetorical question
options.feedback: It is a statement.

options.text: a counter-argument
options.feedback: There is no opposing view.

items.explain: Three parallel phrases sound complete and memorable.
items.hook: Rule of three: things in threes stick. Veni, vidi, vici.
items.example: Slogans love threes: “Stop, look, listen” and “Reduce, reuse, recycle”.

items.prompt: What is the purpose of a rhetorical question?

options.text: To make listeners think rather than reply
To find out what the audience already knows
options.feedback: Real questions do that.

options.text: To give the audience a moment to answer
options.feedback: A rhetorical question does not expect an answer.

items.explain: “Who among us would stay silent?” forces the audience to agree.
items.example: Teachers use them all the time: “Do you really think that is acceptable?”

items.prompt: Why does a good persuasive speech include a counter-argument?

options.text: It makes your case look stronger and fairer
It confuses the audience so they stop disagreeing
options.feedback: It shows you have considered other views.

options.text: Persuasive speeches must always be balanced
options.feedback: It is a rhetorical choice.

items.explain: Acknowledge, then rebut: “Some argue… However…”
items.hook: Acknowledge, then knock it down: “Some say… However…”

items.prompt: Why might a speaker use “we” and “us”?

options.text: To make the audience feel united with the speaker
Because “I” is grammatically incorrect in speeches
options.feedback: Inclusive pronouns are a choice.

options.text: To sound more formal and less personal
options.feedback: It is about unity, not formality.

items.explain: Inclusive pronouns build a sense of shared purpose.
items.example: Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign slogan “Yes we can” is built on an inclusive pronoun.

items.prompt: “I’ve told you a million times!” is an example of…

options.text: hyperbole
statistics
options.feedback: It is deliberate exaggeration, not data.

options.text: understatement
options.feedback: Understatement does the opposite.

items.explain: Hyperbole: from Greek “throwing beyond”.
items.hook: Hyper (over) + ballein (to throw): hyperbole overshoots the truth.

items.prompt: Which Greek philosopher wrote the “Rhetoric”, describing ethos, pathos and logos?
items.explain: Aristotle (384–322 BC) taught Alexander the Great.
items.hook: Socrates taught Plato, Plato taught Aristotle, Aristotle taught Alexander the Great.

items.prompt: Martin Luther King repeated “I have a dream” at the start of several sentences. Why is this effective?

options.text: The repetition builds rhythm and a memorable vision
He had forgotten that he had already said it
options.feedback: It was deliberate anaphora.

options.text: Repeating a phrase makes the speech easier to write
options.feedback: Repetition adds length but also power.

items.explain: Anaphora gives a speech a powerful, memorable refrain. Washington, 1963.
items.example: King gave the speech on 28 August 1963 at the Lincoln Memorial, to a crowd of about 250,000.

items.prompt: Which phrase uses the most emotive language?

options.text: a heartless act of destruction
a planned change to the old building
options.feedback: Neutral and calm.

options.text: some work on the site
options.feedback: Neutral.

items.explain: Emotive language chooses words with strong connotations to provoke feeling.
items.example: Tabloid headlines choose emotive words: “fury”, “horror”, “shame”.

items.prompt: Homer’s Odyssey begins near the end of Odysseus’s journey and tells earlier events later. Starting in the middle of the action is called…

options.text: in medias res
a cyclical structure
options.feedback: That is when the ending echoes the opening.

options.text: a flashback ending
options.feedback: Not a standard term.

items.explain: In medias res is Latin for “into the middle of things”.
items.hook: In medias res: drop the reader into the middle, and explain later.

items.prompt: A story ends in the same place it began, with the character changed. This is a…

options.text: cyclical structure
linear structure
options.feedback: Linear stories move straight through time.

options.text: cliffhanger
options.feedback: A cliffhanger leaves the ending unresolved.

items.explain: A cyclical structure invites the reader to compare the beginning and end.
items.hook: Cyclical = cycle: the story comes back round to where it started.

items.prompt: “The sky wept as the funeral procession passed.” The weather reflecting the mood is called…

options.text: pathetic fallacy
onomatopoeia
options.feedback: No sound words.

options.text: simile
options.feedback: There is no “like” or “as”.

items.explain: Pathetic fallacy (a term coined by John Ruskin) gives nature human feelings that match the mood.
items.example: Ruskin coined the term in Modern Painters in 1856, as a criticism of over-emotional writing.

items.prompt: Which sentence SHOWS fear rather than telling it?

options.text: Mira’s hands trembled; her breath came in short, sharp gasps.
Mira was very scared, more scared than she had ever been.
options.feedback: This tells the emotion directly.

options.text: Mira felt a terrible fear growing inside her.
options.feedback: This names the emotion.

items.explain: Showing uses physical details and actions so the reader infers the emotion.
items.hook: Show, don’t tell: give the reader the evidence and let them work out the feeling.

items.prompt: Why might a writer use a series of short sentences at a climax?

options.text: To speed up the pace and build tension
To slow the story down
options.feedback: Short sentences usually speed things up.

options.text: Because long sentences are wrong
options.feedback: Variety is the key.

items.explain: Short sentences create urgency; longer ones can slow and stretch a moment.
items.hook: Short sentences speed things up. Like a heartbeat. Racing.

items.prompt: An early hint of something that will happen later is called…

options.text: foreshadowing
a flashback
options.feedback: A flashback goes back in time.

options.text: a resolution
options.feedback: The resolution comes at the end.

items.explain: Foreshadowing builds anticipation: the oracle’s warning foreshadows the tragedy.

items.prompt: A narrator whose account the reader cannot fully trust is…

options.text: an unreliable narrator
an omniscient narrator
options.feedback: An omniscient narrator knows everything.

options.text: a second-person narrator
options.feedback: That uses “you”.

items.explain: Unreliable narrators may lie, misunderstand or be biased.

items.prompt: Which narrator knows the thoughts of every character?

options.text: a third-person omniscient narrator
a first-person narrator who sees everything
options.feedback: First-person narrators only know their own thoughts.

options.text: a third-person limited narrator
options.feedback: Limited narrators follow one character’s thoughts.

items.explain: Omniscient means all-knowing, like a god on Olympus looking down.
items.hook: Omni (all) + scient (knowing): the narrator knows everything, like a god on Olympus.

items.prompt: Which description uses the most senses?

options.text: The salt wind stung her lips as gulls shrieked above the rotting nets.
The beach was beautiful and the day was very pleasant.
options.feedback: No sensory detail at all.

options.text: There was a long beach with some birds and a few old boats.
options.feedback: Sight only, and very vague.

items.explain: Taste/touch (salt, stung), sound (shrieked) and smell (rotting) bring the scene alive.
items.hook: The senses checklist: see, hear, smell, taste, touch. Use at least three.

items.prompt: Put the stages of a classic story structure (Freytag’s pyramid) in order.
items.explain: Set-up, build-up, the turning point, the consequences, and the ending.
items.hook: A story mountain: climb up (rising action), reach the top (climax), come down (falling action).

visual.caption: Freytag’s pyramid: tension rises to the climax, then falls away.

items.prompt: Which opening hooks the reader most effectively?

options.text: The monster had been dead for three days when it knocked on our door.
One day I woke up, got dressed and went down to have my breakfast.
options.feedback: Ordinary details do not create intrigue.

options.text: This is a story about a monster that lived near our small village.
options.feedback: It tells rather than intrigues.

items.explain: A strong hook raises a question the reader needs answered.
items.hook: A hook raises a question the reader must have answered.

items.prompt: Which verb is most precise and powerful? “The serpent ___ across the rocks.”

options.text: slithered
went
options.feedback: “went” is vague.

options.text: moved
options.feedback: “moved” is vague.

items.explain: Precise verbs do the work of adjectives and adverbs.
items.hook: A strong verb beats a weak verb + adverb: “slithered” beats “moved slowly”.

items.prompt: “You step into the cave. You hear dripping water.” What is the effect of second-person narration?

options.text: It puts the reader directly into the scene
It makes the story feel more distant and formal
options.feedback: It does the opposite.

options.text: It shows the narrator knows everyone’s thoughts
options.feedback: Second person is close, not all-knowing.

items.explain: Second person (“you”) is rare, immersive and unsettling.
items.example: Choose-your-own-adventure books are written in the second person: “You open the door…”

items.prompt: Which dialogue tag is most effective for a frightened character?

options.text: she whispered
she said
options.feedback: “said” is invisible, which is sometimes fine, but here a verb can show fear.

options.text: she stated
options.feedback: “stated” sounds calm and formal.

items.explain: Well-chosen speech verbs or actions show how words are spoken.
items.hook: “Said” is invisible; whispered, hissed or stammered shows how the words are spoken.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “needed; essential”.
items.explain: necessary. One collar (c), two sleeves (ss).
items.learn: **necessary** (needed; essential). One collar (c), two sleeves (ss).
items.hook: Necessary: one collar (c), two sleeves (ss).

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “apart; to divide”.
items.explain: separate. There is “a rat” in separate.
items.learn: **separate** (apart; to divide). There is “a rat” in separate.
items.hook: There is a rat in sep-a-rat-e.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “without doubt”.
items.explain: definitely. It contains the word “finite”.
items.learn: **definitely** (without doubt). It contains the word “finite”.
items.hook: Definitely has “finite” inside it: de-finite-ly. No a anywhere.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “to make someone feel awkward”.
items.explain: embarrass. Two r’s and two s’s: you go really red and smile shyly.
items.learn: **embarrass** (to make someone feel awkward). Two r’s and two s’s: you go really red and smile shyly.
items.hook: You go Really Red and Smile Shyly: double r, double s.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “to provide room for”.
items.explain: accommodate. It accommodates two c’s and two m’s.
items.learn: **accommodate** (to provide room for). It accommodates two c’s and two m’s.
items.hook: Accommodate is big enough to fit two c’s and two m’s.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “a regular beat”.
items.explain: rhythm. Rhythm Helps Your Two Hips Move.
items.learn: **rhythm** (a regular beat). Rhythm Helps Your Two Hips Move.
items.hook: Rhythm Helps Your Two Hips Move.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “your inner sense of right and wrong”.
items.explain: conscience. con + science.
items.learn: **conscience** (your inner sense of right and wrong). con + science.
items.hook: Con + science: your conscience is your own science of right and wrong.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “something that happens”.
items.explain: occurrence. Double c, double r, and -ence.
items.learn: **occurrence** (something that happens). Double c, double r, and -ence.
items.hook: Occurrence: double c, double r, and it ends -ence.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “a special right or advantage”.
items.explain: privilege. No d: privi-lege.
items.learn: **privilege** (a special right or advantage). No d: privi-lege.
items.hook: There is no ledge in privilege: no d.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “playfully naughty”.
items.explain: mischievous. Three syllables: mis-chie-vous. There is no “i” after the v.
items.learn: **mischievous** (playfully naughty). Three syllables: mis-chie-vous. There is no “i” after the v.
items.hook: Mischief + -ous, with the f turned into v: mischievous. No “-ious”.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “a firm promise”.
items.explain: guarantee. gu-ar-an-tee: the u is silent.
items.learn: **guarantee** (a firm promise). gu-ar-an-tee: the u is silent.
items.hook: A guard guarantees your safety: both begin g-u-a.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “a word that imitates a sound”.
items.explain: onomatopoeia. From Greek: onoma (name) + poiein (to make). Note the -poeia.
items.learn: **onomatopoeia** (a word that imitates a sound). From Greek: onoma (name) + poiein (to make). Note the -poeia.
items.example: Comic-strip sound words are onomatopoeia: BANG, POW, WHOOSH.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “side by side and never meeting”.
items.explain: parallel. The double l in the middle looks like two parallel lines.
items.learn: **parallel** (side by side and never meeting). The double l in the middle looks like two parallel lines.
items.example: The parallel bars in gymnastics: two bars side by side that never meet.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “a thousand years”.
items.explain: millennium. Double l and double n: mille (thousand) + annus (year).
items.learn: **millennium** (a thousand years). Double l and double n: mille (thousand) + annus (year).
items.example: The year 2000 was celebrated as the new millennium; London built the Millennium Bridge.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “to work together and share information”.
items.explain: liaise. Two i’s: li-ai-se.
items.learn: **liaise** (to work together and share information). Two i’s: li-ai-se.
items.hook: Liaise has an i on each side of the a: l-i-a-i-s-e.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “a line of people waiting”.
items.explain: queue. q-ueue: the “ue” comes twice.
items.learn: **queue** (a line of people waiting). q-ueue: the “ue” comes twice.
items.hook: Queue: a q, then four letters waiting in line behind it, u-e-u-e.

items.prompt: “The army of clouds advanced; thunder fired; the trees surrendered.” What technique links these words?

options.text: a semantic field of war
onomatopoeia
options.feedback: Only “thunder” relates to sound, and it is not imitative here.

options.text: a rhetorical question
options.feedback: There are no questions.

items.explain: A semantic field is a group of words linked by meaning; here war imagery makes the storm feel like an attack.
items.hook: A semantic field is a word family united by meaning.
items.example: Food adverts often use a semantic field of comfort: warm, golden, homely, melting.

items.prompt: The word “lair” has connotations of…

options.text: danger and wild predators
comfort and safety
options.feedback: That would be “home” or “nest”.

options.text: wealth
options.feedback: No link to money.

items.explain: Connotations are the associations a word carries beyond its literal meaning (denotation).
items.hook: Denotation = the dictionary meaning; connotation = the feelings that come with it.
items.example: Estate agents say “cosy” rather than “small”: same room, nicer connotation.

items.prompt: “Swords, shields, spears, helmets littered the field.” A list with no conjunctions is…

options.text: asyndetic
syndetic
options.feedback: A syndetic list uses conjunctions.

options.text: polysyndetic

items.hook: Asyndeton is Greek for “unbound”: a list with the “and”s taken out.

items.prompt: “The waves rose and the wind howled and the mast cracked.” The repeated “and” is…

options.text: polysyndeton
asyndeton
options.feedback: Asyndeton removes conjunctions.

options.text: anaphora
options.feedback: Anaphora repeats words at the start of clauses; here it is a conjunction throughout.

items.hook: Poly (many) + syndeton (bound together): many “and”s.

items.prompt: “The serpent slid silently, sly and slow.” The repeated “s” sound is…

options.text: sibilance
plosive alliteration
options.feedback: Plosives are b, p, t, d, k sounds.

options.text: assonance
options.feedback: Assonance repeats vowel sounds.

items.explain: Sibilance can sound sinister, soothing or secretive.
items.hook: Sibilance hisses like a snake: s, sh and soft c sounds.

items.prompt: “Boom! The bronze doors burst, battered by the brute.” The repeated hard “b” sounds are…

options.text: plosive alliteration
sibilance
options.feedback: Sibilance repeats s sounds.

options.text: onomatopoeia only
options.feedback: Only “boom” is onomatopoeic; the pattern is plosive alliteration.

items.explain: Plosive sounds feel harsh, violent or forceful.
items.hook: Plosives burst from the lips and tongue: p, b, t, d, k, g.

items.prompt: “A deafening silence.” This is an…

options.text: oxymoron
euphemism
options.feedback: A euphemism softens something unpleasant.

options.text: allusion
options.feedback: An allusion refers to another text.

items.explain: Oxymoron, from Greek oxys (sharp) + moros (dull): itself an oxymoron!
items.example: “Bittersweet” and “seriously funny” are everyday oxymorons.

items.prompt: “Getting the report finished was a true odyssey.” Referring to another famous text or story is…

options.text: allusion
pathetic fallacy
options.feedback: That is about weather and mood.

options.text: personification
options.feedback: No human qualities are given here.

items.explain: An allusion borrows the meaning of a famous story in a single word.
items.hook: An allusion is a nod to another story: one word borrows its whole meaning.
items.example: Calling a weak spot an “Achilles heel” or a hard trip an “odyssey” are allusions.

items.prompt: A metaphor that continues across a whole paragraph or text is…

options.text: an extended metaphor
a repeated simile
options.feedback: A simile uses like or as.

options.text: a recurring motif
options.feedback: A motif is a repeated image or idea, not one continuous comparison.

items.explain: Extended metaphors develop one comparison in several ways.
items.example: Shakespeare’s “All the world’s a stage” speech stretches one metaphor for life over many lines.

items.prompt: In a structure question, what is a “shift in focus”?

A point where the writer switches to a new font or colour
options.feedback: Structure is about the order and focus of ideas.

options.text: A place where a word is spelt in an unusual or old-fashioned way
options.feedback: Not a structural feature.

items.explain: Structure questions ask how the writer guides the reader’s attention through the text.
items.hook: Think like a film camera: where is it pointing, and when does it move?

items.prompt: Which analysis sentence is strongest?

options.feedback: It names a feature but explains nothing.

options.text: The storm is very violent and the ship is in a lot of danger here.
options.feedback: Too vague: how and why?

items.hook: Quote the word, name the method, explain the effect: “clawed” → a predator.

items.prompt: “Oh, wonderful. Another monster. Just what I needed.” What is the tone?

options.text: sarcastic
delighted
options.feedback: The words are positive, but the meaning is the opposite.

options.text: terrified
options.feedback: The speaker sounds weary, not terrified.

items.explain: Sarcasm says the opposite of what is meant, often to mock.
items.hook: Sarcasm: the words say “wonderful”; the voice says the opposite.

items.prompt: Which connective signals a CONTRAST between two texts?

options.text: whereas
similarly
options.feedback: “similarly” signals a similarity.

options.text: furthermore
options.feedback: “furthermore” adds a point.

items.explain: Contrast: whereas, however, in contrast, conversely. Similarity: similarly, likewise, both.
items.hook: Contrast: whereas, however, conversely. Similarity: similarly, likewise, both.

items.prompt: When comparing texts, what does GAP stand for?

options.text: Genre, Audience, Purpose
Grammar, Accuracy, Punctuation
options.feedback: Those matter, but GAP is about context.

options.text: Gods, Ancients, Poets
options.feedback: A good guess for this course, but no!

items.explain: Ask: what kind of text, for whom, and why?
items.hook: Mind the GAP, like the warning on the London Underground: Genre, Audience, Purpose.

items.prompt: A Victorian travel writer calls a Greek ruin “a sad heap of stones”; a modern guide calls it “breathtaking”. What should a comparison focus on?

Which writer is right about the ruin today
options.feedback: Comparison analyses views; it doesn’t judge which is correct.

options.text: Summarising what each text says, one after the other
options.feedback: You must compare as you go.

items.explain: Compare attitudes and methods together, with evidence from both.

items.prompt: A “summary of differences” question tests what skill?

options.text: Synthesis: combining information from both texts
Spelling and punctuation in a short answer
options.feedback: It tests reading.

options.text: Creative writing inspired by the two texts
options.feedback: It is a reading skill.

items.explain: Synthesis means combining evidence from two sources to make inferences.
items.hook: Synthesis = putting together (syn = together): two texts, one answer.

items.prompt: Which is an OPINION?

The Parthenon stands on the Acropolis in Athens.
options.feedback: That can be checked: a fact.

options.text: The Parthenon was completed in the 430s BC.
options.feedback: That is a historical fact.

items.explain: Facts can be proved; opinions are judgements.

items.prompt: A leaflet about a new hotel on a Greek island is written by the hotel company. What should a careful reader consider?

Everything in it must be true because it is printed

options.text: It is fiction, so none of it can be trusted at all

The road to Delphi climbs and climbs until the olive groves below look like a green sea frozen in waves. Then, suddenly, the mountain opens. Grey cliffs, the Shining Ones, rise straight up behind the ruins, so high that eagles circle beneath their summits. The air is cold and very still.

Nothing moves among the broken columns of the Temple of Apollo. Lizards sun themselves on stones that kings once knelt on. Somewhere water trickles: the Castalian spring, where pilgrims washed before asking their questions. You find yourself whispering, though there is no one to hear.

For a thousand years, people climbed this road with their fears in their hands. Should I marry? Should we go to war? Will my son come home? The answers were famously riddling. Standing here, in the silence, you start to understand why they kept coming anyway.
